1.title: The Center of Mass
1.text:
The Center of Mass

The center of mass is the point on an object that moves the same way a point particle would move.

Our big question for this lesson: why are some vehicles more likely to roll over than others? The answer starts with a special point inside every object.

Toss a wrench, and it might spin around its handle or flip end over end. Does any single point on it travel in a straight line? Look at Figure 16. There is one point, shown by the white dot, whose path is a straight line, as if the whole wrench could be replaced by a single particle sitting there. The point on an object that moves just like a point particle would is called the center of mass.

testIt.name: Toss a wrench
testIt.how: Tap to toss the wrench and switch which point you trace.

2.title: Locating the Center of Mass
2.text:
Locating the Center of Mass

Hang an object from two different points; the center of mass is where the two vertical lines cross.

How do you find an object's center of mass? Hang it from any point. When it stops swinging, the center of mass lies somewhere on the vertical line straight down from the hanging point. Draw that line. Then hang it from a different point and draw a second vertical line. The center of mass is where the two lines cross.

The wrench, and every other object moving freely through space, rotates about an axis that passes through its center of mass. So where do you think your own center of mass is?

4.title: The Human Body's Center of Mass
4.text:
The Human Body's Center of Mass

Your center of mass is a few centimeters below your navel, and it moves when you move your arms and legs.

For a person standing with arms hanging straight down, the center of mass is a few centimeters below the navel, midway between the front and back of the body. On average, it sits a little lower for women than for men. But your body is flexible, so your center of mass isn't fixed. Raise your hands over your head, and it rises 6 to 10 centimeters.

A ballet dancer uses this to seem to float on air. In a leap, she raises her arms and legs, as in Figure 17, moving her center of mass up within her body. Her center of mass still follows a parabola, but her head and torso stay at almost the same height for a surprisingly long time. It's an illusion of floating!

High jumpers use a similar trick called the Fosbury flop. The jumper arches over the bar backward, and their center of mass can actually pass below the bar while their body goes over it. That lets them clear the bar at its highest positions.

testIt.how: Tap to raise or lower the leaper's arms and legs. Compare the paths of the CM and the head.

5.title: Tipping a Box
5.text:
Tipping a Box

An object tips over once its center of mass is no longer above its base of support.

What makes a vehicle stable or prone to roll over? Think about tipping over a box. A tall, narrow box standing on end tips more easily than a low, wide one. Why?

To tip a box, as in Figure 18, you have to rotate it about a corner. You pull at the top with a force F, making a torque tau sub F. The box's weight, acting at its center of mass, makes an opposing torque, tau sub w. When the center of mass is directly above the corner it pivots on, tau sub w is zero, and the only torque is yours. Rotate it a little farther, and the center of mass is no longer above the base. Now both torques point the same way, and the box tips over fast.

testIt.name: Tip a box
testIt.how: Tilt the box over its corner. Its weight first twists it back, then over.

6.title: Stability
6.text:
Stability

An object is stable if a large external force is needed to tip it; a broad base and a low center of mass increase stability.

An object is stable if it takes a large external force to tip it. The box in Figure 18 stays stable as long as the torque from its weight tends to keep it upright, which is true as long as its center of mass is above its base. To tip it, you have to rotate the center of mass around the pivot until it's no longer over the base, and that means lifting the center of mass. The broader the base, the more stable the object. That's why bus riders stand with their feet apart as the bus starts, stops, and weaves through traffic.

Now, the vehicles in Figure 19. The one with the higher center of mass doesn't have to tilt very far before its center of mass is outside its base, and its center of mass doesn't have to be lifted as much. That's our answer: vehicles with a high center of mass, especially on a narrow base, are more likely to roll over. The lower an object's center of mass, the more stable it is.

testIt.name: Tall or low
testIt.how: Tap to switch vehicles. A low, wide vehicle tips at a bigger angle.

7.title: Stability in People
7.text:
Stability in People

An object is most stable when it has a low center of mass above a broad base.

You're stable standing flat on your feet. But stand on tiptoe, and your center of mass moves forward right above the balls of your feet, leaving you very little stability. In judo, aikido, and other martial arts, a fighter uses torque to rotate an opponent into an unstable position, where the opponent's center of mass is no longer above their feet. Applying force in the right place lets a smaller person defend against a stronger one.

In summary: if the center of mass isn't above the base, the object is unstable and will roll over with no added torque. If the center of mass is above the base, it's stable. And if the base is very narrow and the center of mass is high, the object may be stable, but the slightest force will tip it. So an object is most stable when its center of mass is low and its base is broad.

testIt.how: Tap to change the stance and see whether the center of mass stays over the base.

8.title: Conditions for Equilibrium
8.text:
Conditions for Equilibrium

Static equilibrium requires zero net force (translational equilibrium) and zero net torque (rotational equilibrium).

If your pen is at rest, what keeps it there? You could hold it or set it on a desk. Something has to push up on it to balance gravity pulling down. And you have to keep it from rotating.

An object is in static equilibrium when its velocity and angular velocity are zero or constant. That takes two conditions. First, translational equilibrium: the net force on the object must be zero. Second, rotational equilibrium: the net torque on the object must be zero.

testIt.name: Equilibrium check
testIt.how: Tap to add the next force. Both the net force and the net torque must be zero.

9.title: Example Problem 5, Static Equilibrium
9.text:
Example Problem 5, Static Equilibrium

Set the net force and the net torque to zero, choosing the axis where one unknown force acts.

A 5.8-kilogram ladder, 1.80 meters long, rests on two sawhorses. Sawhorse A is 0.60 meters from one end, and sawhorse B is 0.15 meters from the other end. What force does each sawhorse exert on the ladder?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the situation. Choose the axis of rotation where F sub A acts, so the torque from F sub A is zero. Known: m equals 5.8 kilograms, l equals 1.80 meters, l sub A equals 0.60 meters, and l sub B equals 0.15 meters. Unknown: F sub A and F sub B.

Step two: solve. The ladder has constant density, so its center of mass is at the center rung. The net force is F sub A plus F sub B plus negative F sub g, and in translational equilibrium that's zero, so F sub A equals F sub g minus F sub B. Now the torques. Gravity's torque is tau sub g equals negative F sub g r sub g, clockwise. Sawhorse B's torque is tau sub B equals positive F sub B r sub B, counterclockwise. In rotational equilibrium, the net torque is zero, so tau sub B equals negative tau sub g, which means F sub B r sub B equals F sub g r sub g. Solving, F sub B equals r sub g m g over r sub B. Putting that into F sub A equals F sub g minus F sub B gives F sub A equals m g times the quantity 1 minus r sub g over r sub B.

Now the distances. The center of mass is at half of l, which is 0.90 meters from the end, so r sub g equals 0.90 meters minus 0.60 meters, or 0.30 meters. And r sub B equals 0.90 meters minus 0.15 meters, plus 0.90 meters minus 0.60 meters, which is 0.75 meters plus 0.30 meters, or 1.05 meters. So F sub B equals 0.30 meters times 5.8 kilograms times 9.8 newtons per kilogram, all over 1.05 meters, which is 16 newtons. And F sub A equals 5.8 kilograms times 9.8 newtons per kilogram times the quantity 1 minus 0.30 meters over 1.05 meters, which is 41 newtons.

Step three: evaluate. Forces are in newtons, and both are upward. The two forces add up to the ladder's weight, and the sawhorse closer to the center of mass pushes harder. That makes sense!

testIt.name: Sawhorses
testIt.how: Slide sawhorse B. Both support forces update for the 5.8 kg, 1.80 m ladder.

10.title: Rotating Frames of Reference
10.text:
Rotating Frames of Reference

Newton's laws hold only in frames of reference that are not rotating or accelerating.

On a spinning amusement park ride, it feels like a strong force is pushing you outward. A pebble on the ride's floor would slide outward with no outward force pushing it, and it wouldn't move in a straight line relative to the floor. Newton's laws seem to break! That's because your point of view, your frame of reference, is rotating. Newton's laws hold only in frames of reference that aren't rotating or accelerating.

This matters because Earth rotates. Its rotation is too gentle to notice in a classroom or lab, but it strongly affects how the atmosphere moves, and so it shapes our weather and climate.

11.title: Centrifugal "Force"
11.text:
Centrifugal "Force"

The centrifugal "force" is an apparent outward force seen only in rotating frames; nothing actually pushes the object outward.

Fasten one end of a spring to the center of a turntable and attach an object to the other end. As the platform spins, someone riding on it sees the object stretch the spring and might think some force is pulling the object outward. This apparent outward force, seen only in rotating frames, is called the centrifugal "force." It isn't a real force, because nothing physically pushes the object outward.

Someone standing on the ground sees it differently. The object moves in a circle, accelerating toward the center because the spring pulls it inward. That centripetal acceleration is a sub c equals the square of v over r, which can also be written as a sub c equals the square of omega times r. So centripetal acceleration is proportional to the distance from the axis and to the square of the angular velocity. Double the rotational frequency, and the centripetal acceleration becomes four times as big.

testIt.how: Set the spin rate. The spring stretches to supply the centripetal force.

12.title: The Coriolis "Force"
12.text:
The Coriolis "Force"

The Coriolis "force" is an apparent force that seems to deflect moving objects, seen only in rotating frames.

Here's a second effect of rotation, shown in Figure 21. A person standing at the center of a spinning disk throws a ball toward the edge. Ignore the ball's fall and look only at its horizontal motion.

Someone standing off the disk sees the ball travel in a straight line at constant speed. But someone riding on the disk sees the ball follow a curved path. The apparent force that seems to bend a moving object's path, seen only in rotating frames, is called the Coriolis "force." Like the centrifugal "force," it isn't a real force. It seems to exist because we see the motion curve when we're in a rotating frame.

13.title: The Coriolis "Force" on Earth
13.text:
The Coriolis "Force" on Earth

In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis "force" deflects moving objects to the right.

Fire a cannon from the equator at a target due north. Because Earth rotates, the projectile also has an eastward velocity, and that eastward speed is greater at the equator than anywhere else. So as the projectile flies north, it moves east faster than the ground beneath it, and it lands east of the target, as in Figure 22. Someone watching from space would just see Earth turning, but an observer on Earth could say the Coriolis "force" pushed the projectile off course. For objects moving toward the equator, the apparent force points west, so a projectile fired due south lands west of its target.

The Coriolis "force" also sets the direction of winds. Winds flow from high pressure toward low pressure. In the Northern Hemisphere, winds from the south get deflected east of a low-pressure area, and winds from the north get deflected west of it. So winds circle counterclockwise around low-pressure areas in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

That's why tropical cyclones, also called hurricanes, spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Hurricanes Katia, Irma, and Jose, from the start of this module, all formed in the Northern Hemisphere, so they spun counterclockwise.

testIt.name: Fire north or south
testIt.how: Tap to fire north or south from the Northern Hemisphere and see where it lands.
